title: Deterministic early-trim admission with tenant cost-fairness
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Background: During multi-region surge events we observe unfair cost amplification: long-running or high-token requests from noisy tenants monopolize GPU cycles and KV cache residency, causing SLO violations for latency-sensitive tenants. Existing probabilistic shedding and client-level token-buckets are reactive and can produce noisy eviction patterns that increase tail latency.

Proposal summary: Implement a deterministic early-trim admission controller that: (1) scores incoming requests on a combined 'cost-fairness' metric (estimated tokens * tenant weight / recent error credit), (2) applies an early-trim policy to requests predicted to exceed per-request token budgets (trimming generation length and structured output fields before they enter the serving queue), and (3) coordinates with a KV-cache trimming signal to preferentially evict cache entries associated with low-priority tenants. The primary goal is to reduce tail latency and keep 99th percentile latency within region SLOs during sustained overload while preserving a predictable degradation model for different tenant tiers.
acceptance_criteria: When load > 85% of provisioned capacity, 99p tail latency for P95-sensitive routes decreases by >= 20% compared to baseline without early-trim
High-cost tenants see predictable trimmed responses (fields removed or shortened) instead of causing full request failures
KV cache eviction rate shifts toward low-priority tenant keys during sustained overload (measured and auditable)
Feature toggles exist to enable/disable early-trim and to adjust tenant-weight curves without deploy
Instrumentation emits cost-fairness score and an admission decision tag per request for postmortem analysis
tasks: Design: define cost-fairness score formula and tenant weight config (PM + Reliability)
Runtime: implement pre-queue admission hook that computes score and canonicalizes request for early-trim
Model-aware trimming: small library of model-specific trimming heuristics (chat vs. single-turn completion vs. embedding)
KV cache integration: signal to cache-manager to evict low-priority keys and to mark keys as 'candidate for trim'
Circuit breaker interaction: ensure admission honors open circuit state and gracefully downgrades to early-trim rather than dropping
Console: add dashboard panels for cost-fairness distribution and per-tenant trimmed-response rate
E2E tests: synthetic workload harness to simulate multi-region surge and assert SLO improvements
Docs: operator runbook with escalation steps and config knobs
rollout_plan: Feature gated behind runtime flag; start disabled in prod
Stage 1 (canary): enable for 5% of traffic in us-west-2 on a single shard for 24h; monitor latency and tail error rates
Stage 2 (regional pilot): enable for 25% of traffic in one region with real tenants paying P2/P3 tiers; run for 72h
Stage 3 (wide): enable for all P3 traffic and 10% of P2 traffic; continue metric-driven expansion
Rollback: immediate flag off to revert to baseline; circuit-breaker fallback always preserves correctness
Operator commands: one-line toggles and per-tenant weight overrides in Console
metrics: 99th and 95th latency by route and tenant tier
Trimmed-response rate per tenant (count and tokens saved)
KV cache churn by tenant pre/post feature
Request rejection rate and circuit-breaker trips

notes: Tradeoffs: deterministic trimming reduces variance but can introduce perceived unfairness if tenant weights are misconfigured. Plan includes conservative defaults and an operator-facing simulation tool.
We intentionally avoid removing fields that would break schema-driven downstream consumers; trimming is primarily length/verbosity or optional descriptive fields first.
Does not replace existing probabilistic shedding — intended to complement it. The admission controller can co-exist and will prefer deterministic early-trim when enabled.
Future: consider integrating billing-tier credit balances and business-pricing signals into cost-fairness score for commercial SLAs.
